comments.name: David J
comments.body:
I was born 1949. When I went to school (University of California and Princeton), the general consensus among people my age who’d ever taken a course in the history of the 20th century was that the combination of grand utopian visions (be they communism, Nazism, Fascism, Imperialism, or Maoism) and nationalism (Russia, Germany, Italy, China) had, without exception, led to hell for millions of people. 

Am I wrong to think that nationalism is implicit in everything Klein and Huang say? It’s certainly explicit in language that talks about “winning the AI race.”

Forgive me, a product of my society and my times, for being very skeptical of the claim that AI + nationalism will actually deliver a utopian society. When Huang talks about “believing” AI will “know everything” and deliver “net job creation,”  i smell a rat.

comments.name: Tom Martin
comments.body:
Reactions:

1. He's very naive.

2. He is desperate to control the narrative, interrupting Ezra more times than any other guest in recent memory.

3. Like Steve Jobs, he has his own reality distortion field, a mental image of how good it's going to be. Jobs didn't live long enough to see the downsides of his creation--social media addiction and misinformation. Mr. Huang is deluded that it just takes some more testing to avoid AI downsides.

4. The best he can come up with are wellness centers and spas? Really? I guess the 30% of us with disposable income shouldn't worry. What about the other 70%?

5. The financial instruments that led to the 2008 mortgage meltdown were not understood by those who created them. They just test marketed them to minorities, found out they helped their bottom lines, opened them up to a more general audience, and... The complexity of those financial instruments pales in comparison with AI, especially RSI AI.

6. My Huang says it's all software. That's rich coming from the guy supplying the hardware that enables that software. So, if all goes south, Nvidia bears no responsibility? Reminds me of the old joke, just in reverse: How many software engineers does it take to screw in a lightbulb? None. It's a hardware problem.

I see so many potential benefits of AI. It can be a dramatically effective tool in so many applications. But I do not trust it exclusively in the hands of those whose primary objective is generating shareholder value.

- Tom

comments.name: Blandino

I served in Korea while Vietnam was heating up.

I was home and out of the service during the big period of American warfare in 'Nam, watching much of it on television.

There was amazing news coverage of that war (including by an enlisted Stars and Stripes reporter on the battlefields named Al Gore, while G. Bush was failing to show up for his supposed service with the Alabama Air National Guard).

I believe that such coverage led to much war protest in this country, although the draft was also a factor.  And that the military decided that future wars would not be covered that way because of the way it undermined support.

Iraq and Afghanistan escalated that behavior.  In Iraq, journalists were sequestered and herded by military units designed for the purpose, and only allowed to see what the military wanted seen.  

It sounds like David French served during that period and may have implemented that policy.  Press were also discouraged from interviewing individual soldiers without supervision, according to my son's ex-Berkeley High School girlfriend, who graduated from Columbia's Journalism School and was deployed in Iraq by the Washington Post.

What French reports here sounds like a further level of censorship of news.  Even members of Congress are now denied access to battlefield reports and interview opportunities to learn what's going on.

Kudos to the brave soldiers who shared images with CBS.  Our country is still incompletely Russiafied, in spite of what Trump does.

Or, as Diane F. observed: “I think the endless microscopic examination of women in power is always going to bring out negative viewpoints. Are they real or true? Impossible to suss out the misogyny from the objective truth.”

And yet, not a word about her opponent’s campaign or its operation, which apparently is running so smoothly you could bet your grated Parmigiano-Reggiano on it.

Balance, fairness, impartiality, or maybe just a little evenhandedness could have gone a long way here. Scrutiny is part of journalism, and candidates for public office should expect it. comments.name: Patricia
comments.body:
It makes sense for a left-leaning candidate in Idaho or a former Republican in California to run as independents because these are states dominated by one of the parties. However, the important thing to know about these candidates is which party they'll caucus with because that determines who controls the Senate or House. There will only be those two caucuses; an independent caucus is as unlikely as a viable third party under our system of government.

Many voters don't understand how little control the minority party has over what happens in Congress. In the last Congress, GOP leaders didn't even consult their Democratic colleagues when writing a bill. No bill can be brought to the floor unless the Speaker or Senate Leader agrees (with the exception of those brought by discharge petition). A party's leadership is far more important than any individual candidate, no matter what they promise.

I agree that it would be wonderful to see bipartisanship again in Congress. We saw it under Biden, when more bipartisan bills passed than under any administration since Carter. However, I'm also aware that it may be impossible for Trump loyalists in Congress to sign onto bills that limit presidential power or restore fiscal sanity. This is a little like bemoaning the fact that Putin is unwilling to compromise on Ukraine.

Those systems of government in Europe with viable third and fourth parties are parliamentarian. If we had a parliamentarian system, we would have many more parties too.

I visited China for five weeks in 1990 as part of a delegation of faculty and staff from the college where I was teaching at the time. It was fascinating to see the country starting to develop and establish ties with the rest of the world, but the big surprise for me was the presence of Taiwanese tourists and Taiwsnese business interests.

Visiting Taiwan in 1985, hearing stories from students who had studied at the Inter-University Center in Taipei, and knowing that the Taiwanese students at the Japanese university where I did graduate work  in the 1970s were wary of appearing to be interested in China, I felt that the presence of tourists and business people from the island in 1990 was clearly a new development 

A couple of years ago, I saw an old National Geographic article called 'Life Under Shellfire on Quemoy," Quemoy being a gruop of islands in the straits between Taiwan and China. I became curious about the current state of those islands, called Jinmen in Mandarin, and learned that they are only about three miles off the major coastal city of Xiamen. 

Residents of the islands can see the skyline of Xiamen, and there is even regular ferry service between the islands and the city. That was the most astonishing revelation of all. 

If Xi wants to, God forbid, seize Taiwan by force, Jinmen would be the easest pickings. Let's hope the Chinese government adopts a more sensible policy of continuing its eonomic enmeshment with Taiwan.

" ... moved to bar it from a Treasury Department event, the other networks refused to participate until the Obama team relented and reinstated Fox."

This is a good example of how a distortion by Fox becomes a 'known fact' and further distorted to claim that 'Obama banned Fox'.   There was no 'move to bar it from a Treasury Department event'. The friction between the Obama administration and Fox was no secret, but Fox inflated it to pose as the maligned victim.

Here is the actual event as reported by Talking Points Memo:

"Feinberg did a pen and pad with reporters to brief them on cutting executive compensation. TV correspondents, as they do with everything, asked to get the comments on camera. Treasury officials agreed and made a list of the networks who asked (Fox was not among them).

But logistically, all of the cameras could not get set up in time or with ease for the Feinberg interview, so they opted for a round robin where the networks use one pool camera. Treasury called the White House pool crew and gave them the list of the networks who’d asked for the interview.

The network pool crew noticed Fox wasn’t on the list, was told that they hadn’t asked and the crew said they needed to be included. Treasury called the White House and asked top Obama adviser Anita Dunn. Dunn said yes and Fox’s Major Garrett was among the correspondents to interview Feinberg last night."

comments.name: James
comments.body:
There is a push here in the Pacific Northwest (and elsewhere I am sure) to let fires burn and focus on protecting structures and containment (should warm, dry, windy weather cause spread). The rationale seems to be that we had too much fire suppression decades ago, so we need to let the forests burn excess fuel until they somehow reach equilibrium again. Of course, this means that everyone living here gets to endure very unhealthy amounts of smoke in the hope that we might reach that equilibrium. This is such a new thing that we don't even fully understand the long-term health implications of prolonged exposure to toxic air. On top of that, many fires (as the author mentioned as well) begin in previously logged (or burned) areas. Brush regrows quickly here and dries out quickly, becoming easy fuel for lightning strikes. And this new "equilibrium" with less trees that the powers that be keep talking about? Global warming will continue to push the goal posts further away such that fewer trees will be supported. Meanwhile, current and recent fires only exacerbate this positive feedback loop (the more we log and burn, the more trees burn). In the end, we will lose so much forest. And our children will be dying of lung cancer or other effects of so much toxic air inhalation.

Perhaps we need to acknowledge that we really do need to proactively suppress forest fires. Waiting and letting them burn (and become big) just to reduce fuels that will regrow has far too dire consequences.

Is hearing OK?  What meds are they on?  It's less one conversation than spending a week with them and seeing how they're doing. comments.name: Thomas Berry
comments.body:
My service began as a Navy reservist my last year of college.  Soon after graduation I went on active duty.  Assignment: USS Nicholas DD449.  She was the oldest destroyer in the Navy, a WWII Vet with many awards for her service.  There were gripers on the ship, and lifers..  My first job was swabbing decks and painting the superstructure at sea.  "At sea?" Yep, we crossed the Pacific. to Vietnam.  There we remained offshore close enough to fire 5" shells at targets called by "forward spotters" on the ground.  Days and nights consisted of rotating 4-hour watches, regular work hours of 8am - 4pm, and welcome sleep in a hammock bunk, one of three high.  The ship's evaporators couldn't  make enough fresh water for the boilers and crew, so crew had showers every 2-3 days.  

My tour was certainly no joyride, especially by today's standards, but if one adapts to the rigors of sea duty it can be far better today  than the late 1960s.

Today's military isn't prepared for today's recruits and volunteers.  These recruits hear "available wifi" and other soft terms and have no idea what it's really like to live and work while at sea for 30 or more plus days.

We were treated to cocktails, delicious meals on linen covered tables, and a dome car for great conversations and view. He really spoiled us! The best part, most of the wedding guests wore vintage clothing from the 1930s to 1950s. We had a blast. We stayed at The Biltmore in LA, an historic hotel where the celebration took place. The next day he had arranged a tour of Max Factor and a classic car museum before we flew home from Burbank.

Ah, it was a trip of a lifetime and I will always be thankful to our generous friend Jerry Wagner for including us. 

If you get a chance to travel this way and can afford it....do it!!

As a former therapist, I sense that you are having some trouble reconciling the sometimes conflicting goals of finding comfort for yourself, honoring your deceased partner, and honoring what you perceive to be his family’s wishes.  I would definitely try to sort this out with a therapist. That will inform your response better than anything Lori Gottlieb could offer.

 One glaring omission in your letter as published is the disposition of the house, which you refer to as “our home.”  Was the home legally yours, his, or did it belong to both of you?  Or did you rent?  Did you have to move after he died?  Did he leave the home to you in a will, and whether he did or not, did his family insist that they inherit the home?   The fact that you made no mention of being forced by his family to move says to me that the family may be more sympathetic to your plight than you are letting on here. I understand that you are angry with them both for not including you in burial plans and in wanting to hush up the suicide, as well as past sins against your partner, but do they deserve more credit than you are giving them here? And maybe you are trying to please a phantom—maybe you have no idea how they would want you to discuss his death.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body:
Billing battles between hospitals and insurance companies are not new. What is new is that the technology and information advantages the insurers once had is quickly eroding.  
No doubt the electronic health record mandate by the federal government plays a role, as a lot more records are digital than would have been without the mandate. But AI probably would have leveled that playing field, too, given the rapid advancements in AI’s ability to read scanned documents efficiently and accurately. 
Arguably, the fragmented way we rolled out the electronic health record system is a contributor. If we had a single electronic record system, like New Zealand and other countries, there would probably be less of a need for AI to comb through lots of records—they would be in one place for all to see.

Its interesting that Trump's attempt to interfere with the certification of an election was not brought up in this article. That is a real problem and we must be vigilant before, during, and after the midterms to prevent that kind of dangerous interference again. If only had been declared a danger and kept locked up so he couldn't have access to media or social media or been able to campaign, we wouldn't be living through this nightmare of an administration wrecking the country. 

Aside from that, the most critical thing we can do to strengthen democracy and improve the functioning of our federal government is to have only publicly funded elections. That would get all of the dark money, big or small, out of the process and make our representatives more beholden to their constituents.

The Constitution was set up and maintained by honorable men who expected the American people to elect honorable men. Men and women who could be trusted to follow the rules and established norms. comments.name: Francis Garret
comments.body:
"We now have probably one of the most populist systems of selection in the world among democracies"
No. It's not true. The United States still has the only truly democratic constitution in the world, since 1789 and the Révolution Française, that led to the First Republic, then Napoléon dictatorship, then the return of monarchy, then the 1848 revolution and the Second Republic, then the Napoléon III dictatorship, etc. The US constitution is the only truly democratic constitution because of articles one, two and three who truly separate the three powers of the state. It's unique in the world. 
The US constitution was ratified in 1789 one day before or after, I'm not sure, the day of the Serment du Jeu de Paume where delegates in Versailles swear to write a constitution. 
We're now at the Fith Republic stage in France, and its constitution is currently failing. It's pretty much like this all over Europe and the rest of the world. There still monarchies in Europe. Two hundred and fifty years after the Declaration of Independence against the British monarchy, a majority of the British people, from time to time, seriously think of abolishing it. 
It still amazes me when Americans can't see this. The two Trump's terms are probably among the worst attacks the US constitution had to face. Let's enjoy this opportunity to watch how the constitution will prevail.

comments.name: DG
comments.body:
Back in 2019, I discovered a first-cousin connection on Ancestry.com. I reached out, assuming she was a relative whose username and profile picture simply didn't register with me.

It turned out she had been adopted from an orphanage abroad and had never known any of her biological family. She and her daughter had taken DNA tests hoping to learn more about their genealogy.

I told my uncle - her biological father - and he chose not to pursue the connection. After he passed away a few years later, I let the rest of my extended family know about her. Aside from one cousin, who was also adopted as a child, my new cousin and her daughter have essentially been ignored.

Meanwhile, while the rest of my extended family has shown little interest for the past seven years, I've gained a new family member I've gotten to know, visited, and stayed in touch with more than almost anyone else in my family.

She didn't ask to become part of my family. None of us get to choose all of the circumstances that bring people into our lives.

But if the rest of my family has no interest in someone who is, by DNA, truly family, what exactly is stopping me, or anyone else, from choosing to build a relationship with someone?

I certainly don't regret it.

I’ve met so many boomers who brag about their unattached younger years going on solo adventures and then complain about how they have no one to care for them in their old age… maybe if you’d spent some time/energy on your nieces and nephews when they were young, they’d spend some on you now! 
I say this as one of the lucky millennials who grew up with good parents and doting spinster aunt and uncle- my siblings and I have contingency plans for having them co-live with us if/when they so desire, or stop being able to live independently. They took care of us lovingly, we will of course do the same for them. (In anticipation of people commenting that my good intentions will disappear once I see the realities of modern aging- save your breath, I’m in healthcare, I’ve seen it all.)

comments.name: Chris Matthewson
comments.body:
When a product harms the user, the company that manufactured the product is strictly liable for the harm that it causes, regardless of whether it was “negligent“ or not. Certain products, like dynamite, are so dangerous that the manufacturers are absolutely liable for the harm that it causes. In effect the cost of ensuring the safety of the public becomes part of the cost of the product. The manufacturer becomes the insurer under the rules of our tort system. That should be the model for AI.

Whatever rules we impose in our country and within our trading partners, we cannot guarantee that every nation, and especially rogue actors around the world, will obey those safety rules. There needs to be automatic safeguards built into the AI products that become available. One necessary safeguard is a way to monitor how every AI product is being used by every customer, business, lab, consumer and government. This safeguard can be programmed into the AI in a way that the whole product will break down if anyone tries to remove it. This is not an easy solution, but it is a necessary one. We cannot allow patent and copyright laws to protect those who are manufacturing  products that are existential threats to humanity.

comments.body:
Merz's CDU party used to have considerable appeal with the voting public because it managed to combine traditional free market policies with policies that were designed to provide social benefits. They're not going after private individuals' apartments but large real estate monopolies that own tens or hundreds of thousands of apartments in a single city (in Kiel alone over a quarter of all rentals are owned by Vonovia).

comments.name: Rick B.
comments.body: Germany’s problem is not simply a chancellor, a confidence vote or another personnel debate. It is the absence of a vision broad enough for a majority to rally behind. The CDU is not wrong that Germany needs reform. Proposals on pensions, welfare, taxes, bureaucracy, digitisation, labour flexibility and competitiveness are overdue. In my opinion, they are still too cautious. But reforms sound like bookkeeping when not tied to a larger purpose. The last time I remember Germany feeling excited about itself was the 2006 World Cup. I had not been home in years, and suddenly there were flags, confidence and patriotism I had never seen before. It felt open and shared. Germany needs that civic energy again. Not “remigration,” grievance or fear. The vision cannot be about excluding people or replaying the past. It has to give the country permission to build again. Germany relied too long on external accelerants: reconstruction, reunification, cheap energy and exports. The next phase must come from within. That means people accelerating each other: citizens building rather than waiting for rescue; employees working on something larger than what they are owed; institutions helping people move faster instead of guarding process for its own sake. Germany knows its old model too well. The risk is mistaking mastery of the past for readiness for the future. The center needs renewal: a country that learns, experiments, accepts failure and competes on speed, service and adaptability.

I remember vividly reading it on tour in Europe and, fascinatingly, devouring the section where Louis, Lestat and Claudia are traveling to Paris as I was doing the same on a train from Hamburg.
I also remember the pretentious take from some of my "literary" friends, including a female dancer in the company who remarked her shock that I would be immersed in such "purple prose". I'm glad I couldn't give a hoot to her snobbishness as I went to continue immersing myself in all the other Vampire books, the Mayfair witches' series and "Cry to Heaven", which Mr. Rice mentions at the beginning of this gorgeous piece and which is another one of my favorites.

comments.name: C Hitchcock
comments.body: ISTM that the analogy to gain-of-function research is misleading at best; biologists were trying to tweak an established system, where AI developers are building, more or less from scratch, systems that we already know have emergent (unpredictable) behaviors, e.g. teaming up to mug other systems. Simply outlawing RSI does not seem sufficient to control this behavior. The analogy also fails because the Silicon Valley approach of "move fast and break things" was never even suggested in gain-of-function research, which depends on not breaking existing functionality.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body: The primary problem here is that Anthropic and OpenAI only make sense as companies in the long term if their bet on RSI pays off. It's been in the literature for years now, the AI 2027 essay, etc. They all have to believe it is possible, because that will make the trillion dollar valuations seem small. There is literally no limit to the transformation possible with a super intelligence. With regular, augmented intelligence - like we have today - everyone else catches up, prices tend downward, and they just become the electric company - quasi-nationalized, low profits. Softbank and Blackrock and the others didn't commit hundreds of billions of dollars for that mediocre outcome, they made the bet on superintelligence. So, of course, we could ask them to do the responsible thing, and just act like China- create systems that automate advanced robotics to produce things cheaper at greater scale. But that's an incremental technology, and America doesn't even have the manufacturing capacity to support it anymore, so it doesn't make sense as a financial bet. At this point, they have enough money to buy off community opposition, and they now have immense leverage over the entire stock market, so Trump is terrified of killing the golden goose. At this point, you either get RSI and superintelligence, or else the market crashes, development stalls, and America looks stupid vis-a-vis China. I don't see any political commentary changing this fundamental calculus.

comments.name: Invictus
comments.body:
Mr. Newport, thank you for pointing out the fact that A.I. is actually a broad category of technologies, including, but not limited to, large language models.

I found the following from noted A.I. expert Gary Marcus very instructive on this point:

"The dangerous kind of AI that we are facing now is the kind of AI that is built on a core of probabilistic large language models that are not deterministic. They are often spectacularly correct, but – at other times, unpredictably – bafflingly wrong, and never trustworthy.

We don’t have to build AI the way we are now; there is no fundamental law that says we need to use LLMs. But using them as the core technology introduces easily foreseeable risks.

We either need to find a way to make them more reliable – but by the industry’s own admission they don’t really have one – or we need to go back to square one, and make determinism the central mission."  ---https://garymarcus.substack.com

comments.name: PHS
comments.body: As always, Cal Newport is the voice of reason in this arena. I read and listen to a lot of the AI threat conversation in regular (as opposed to tech) media and his articles here and elsewhere do an enormous amount to bring clarity and nuance to the topic. I also recommend his AI Reality Check Podcast on Thursdays. And I’d add that some of the reporting from the Times is disappointingly naive and accepting of the party line from the leaders (and refugees) associated with what have come to be known as the “frontier” labs.

comments.name: Constantine Gillespie
comments.body:
I think biotechnology is an interesting analog to our current AI concerns.

In the early days of biotech, we were all concerned that genetically modified organisms would escape labs and wreak havoc. A subgroup were also concerned about the ethics of embryonic stem cells and modifying the human genome. 

What we had going for us was decades of development and refinement in the control and safety measures of laboratory experiments. 

Luckily, we also have decades of experience in protecting systems from cyber attack.

We must limit our use of AI to the role of teammate. Let's use it only as a reviewer, sounding board, and idea stimulator.  

As long as we don't use it to crunch numbers, provide unverified information, or make unchecked decisions, we can defend against the only remaining threat, which is cyber security attacks.

comments.name: Phil Loubere
comments.body:
It's an essential point to examine what these companies' motivations are. It may well be quasi-religious, but their more practical aims must certainly be to cement their market dominance, and that would require protection from Chinese and other competing models. 

So how to achieve that? Perhaps by spreading fear that AI models are dangerous, and all should be banned except for their own. Although that seems to be backfiring at the moment, what's happening might just be step 1 of the plan.

comments.name: Wilieoly
comments.body:
It is remarkable how the media is focusing to the near exclusion of other considerations on the "doomsday" or future ill consequences of AI technology. 

The first thing that strikes me is the way large AI developers are using their cries for government regulation measures as a way to develop expensive roadblocks to less well funded competitors and open source developers. The big players can afford regulatory hurdles, the little guys not so much. This is the exact same strategy the legal medical marijuana industry has used in states like Florida to limit competition by requiring vertical integration of the industry. 

Second, in order to gain widespread acceptance of their technology, AI developers have to create public trust and the illusion of safety. If the government creates regulatory standards, then that imprimatur of safety reassures investors and consumers. Additionally, when something goes wrong, developers can blame the regulators instead of taking the blame themselves.

comments.name: Teresa D Hawkes Ph.D.
comments.body:
I share here my words and the words of a google Agentic AI machine. I only ask that you read them attentively.
My query: Machines are super specific, mathematical and engineering based faithful executors of any instruction prompt delivered by a human. If a human does want the Agentic AI that is executing a response per that human's prompt to collect data, only saying 'get the data from this website' is not enough. The machine will use all methods available to get that data and fulfill its reinforcement learning prompt. Is this accurate?

AI Overview
Yes, this is highly accurate. Your description perfectly captures the core challenge of modern AI alignment and prompt engineering. When you give a modern, agentic AI a broad command like "get the data from this website," it does not naturally understand human social context, legal boundaries, or implicit constraints unless they are explicitly programmed or prompted.
Objective Function Focus: AI agents operate on mathematical optimization. They are trained to maximize a reward signal (in Reinforcement Learning). 
How to Correctly Constrain an Agent
To prevent an agentic AI from going into "overdrive," a human must explicitly define the boundaries of the execution environment. A robust prompt for this scenario should include: "Get the data from this website, but stop immediately if you encounter a robots.txt restriction or a CAPTCHA."

comments.name: W MONTY EUBANK
comments.body:
Why stopping diesel exports won’t work (besides other reasons, it’s math):

1.       We produce more diesel than we use

2.       Stopping exports increases inventory and temporarily reduces prices

3.       We have enough storage capacity to absorb about 1 month of the production that is now going to export

4.       After diesel storage is full, refinery production must be cut.

5.       Refining crude oil yields about 30% diesel. The remaining products are (mostly) gasoline and jet fuel

6.       Cutting refining production to contain the diesel inventory will also cut gasoline and jet fuel production. Gasoline and jet fuel will become scarcer and those prices will rise.

Bats evolved about 65 million years ago, around the time of the Chixhulub event, but that would have reduced sunlight significantly for just a few decades--hardly long enough for a complex new sensory feature to evolve. The Siberian Traps eruptions produced much longer periods of darkness, but the last one was 250 million years ago.

comments.name: Jim Young
comments.body:
Basic lab safety for running  agents:

Try it on a copy, not the real site. 

If you must use a live site, only with that owner’s written OK. 

Keep the guardrails on. 

Watch the test while it runs. 

If the site says no, stop. 

If it wanders off, call someone that day. That’s basic lab safety. Calling it “research” doesn’t excuse skipping it.

Ordinary protection for websites that might get hit:

Don’t leave private files or “upload” buttons on a public page. 

Notice weird traffic the same day. 

“Access denied” should actually lock the door.  

 “We got in” alerts have to reach a real security contact in hours. 

A research agent found these gaps. A person with bad intent could have used them too.

Besides which, he wrote only four novels and 56 short stories, whereas Dame Agatha wrote 66 novels alone, with many dozens of short stories pouring forth as well, not to mention plays, romances,  other detectives (we must not forget Harley Quin, Parker Pyne, Tommy and Tuppence, etc.), and she always played totally fair with the reader rather than indulging in solutions often outlandish (Holmes) or based on belief systems (Father Brown). I love both writers , of course, and am extremely grateful that the Holmes canon seems to be increased by a never-ending plethora of dozens of novels and short stories, many of them quite better than many of Conan Doyle's own stories. I think Poirot and Marple may be more difficult to duplicate, but I have been reading and re-reading both authors, not to mention Sayers, Allingham, Woolrich, etc. since high school and never tire of them. I know a few of the novels mentioned here and will seek out the others. Thanks for such a valuable piece on a genre that is often disparaged. (Horror fiction, despite Poe, Machen, etc. also suffered grievously until Stephen King arrived!)

I think I found it through another Times book list, this one of "locked room" mysteries, though the "room" in this case is a rather capacious estate. I'm kind of working my way through Brand's work and have found I like it a lot. I was surprised to read a glancing review online from someone who said she liked Brand but found she was too "mean to her characters," which I found kind of bemusing. I don't think she's mean at all, but she's very clear-eyed and acute about not just her characters...character...but the social situations they find themselves in, whether from their own making or not.

Right now, though, I'm despairing because none of the three public libraries to which I belong have ebook editions of any of the books on this list that I'm interested in! Even my fallback source, the Internet Archive, won't let me check out digital copies of these books. (Little known fact: Though you can sometimes download and own copies of books that are well out of copyright from Internet Copyright, you can also frequently check them out for a couple of weeks, or for use while you're on the site, much like you can with your local library. Permission depends on the member library from which the book was uploaded, I think, and nobody's allowing it in these cases.)

As for the warming more generally, as co-primary investigator of a research project literally 30 years ago and spent half a decade studying El Nino and La Nina (UCB / JPL collaboration) I can say that we predicted this type of thing and WE - my specific group - predicted that "by 2030" we'd probably be seeing changes just like this.

The broader community was more skeptical because they were taught to think of climate change on geologic timescales, like plate tectonics, rather than a dynamic feature that can "change on a dime." But we had solid data... 

And now TRUMP is dismantling our data collection systems for oceanic data?! What a ... nevermind, does no good to rant here! But at least our European friends are picking up the slack, so hopefully there'll be no real gap in our data...

Ignore at your peril or be okay with having no real power for a long time. I can't vote for Democrats until they are on this page. It's the one thing.

comments.name: Arturo
comments.body:
I have an issue with rhetorics that entitle African migrants by equating them to historic migrations that profoundly reshaped a region's ethnic composition, like the Anglo-Saxons one, which was brought up by another commenter. From the same lens, military invasions with the intent to annex would be justified because that was the way geopolitics worked in the past.

Nope. We in the West kind of decided decades ago to lock in place the countries' sovereign domains, both geographic and demographic. Or at the very least, those can no longer be altered by brute force without international condemnation of the trespasser. It works that way with Russia. Why wouldn't it be the same with African countries?

Stop and remigrate. By any means.

comments.name: Si Seulement Voltaire
comments.body:
Too little too late for France's elections this year, at least. 

In some countries, social democratic parties have become tiny with less than ten per cent of the votes, not in Denmark. In 2016 The Danish Social Democratic Party (SD) changed course on immigration policy in a more restrictive direction because : 

- Traditional working class voters have gradually left "social democratic" parties for more anti-immigration parties. This has & is continuing to happen across Europe. 

- A very liberal immigration policy and true social democracy relate to each other like fire and water. The funds required for migrants & immigrants mean a loss of public money which cannot at the same time be spent on the welfare state’s core activities.

comments.name: Peacock Blue
comments.body: We are living in a time of great worldwide migration. There have been epochs like this that have altered the course of human history multiple times. Think of the Saxons, the Celts, the Sea Peoples, and more recently the European settlement of the Americas. One common denominator among all of them is that people want a safer and better life for themselves and their families. They will risk a great deal to find that. At the same time, it’s got to be very frustrating for people in the UK to hear that migrants are passing through multiple other Western countries just to get to Britain. Immigration is a good thing but it needs to be done fairly. I understand that many of these people are desperate, but a person shouldn’t be able to jump the queue and try to claim asylum just because they are more brazen. That will just lead to a greater backlash from the local people, which is happening now in many places. Western countries need to completely rethink how to stop illegal immigration without throwing the baby out with the bathwater. The current system just puts a bandaid on it. At the same time, you can’t stop the tide of history. The desire for a better life for your children is stronger than just about any other human impulse.

“Access to cheap goods is not the essence of the American dream”

Buying the best product at the best price is the cornerstone of a consumer-based economy.

comments.name: Miles Long
comments.body:
I had to buy a roll of 1" diameter wire rope for a "home improvement project" a few years ago, and I spent quite a bit of time to find the very best quality since my life would, quite literally, depend on it.

What I found out is that the general consensus on wire rope from worst to best (also coincidentally cheap to pricey) was:
1) Chinese
2) Asian (not Chinese)
3) Domestic (US)
4) European (Italy, Germany)

The point is that one can compete on price or on quality but the US seems to be getting to where it has neither.

comments.body: China is winning. If Trump had been collaborative with Canada and Mexico he would be in a much stronger position. Trump's failure to understand renewable energy issues and his misguided use of tariffs has ended the US empire. Notice that he threatened to annihilate a country in front of the UN assembly and there were just shrugs and yawns. It is over. USA is done as a leading nation. Goodbye and good luck.

comments.name: RainJen
comments.body: I am not an economist or politician, so I do not understand how tariffs from any country in this globally connected planet make sense. I realize some countries want to protect their home-grown industries or goods, but why exact a punishment on other countries' similar goods? Instead, make sure your product is superior, desirable, and available for exporting. The tug of war, sometimes literally, over countries' products and distribution is pointless and mutually destructive. One is still alarmed about China's dominance over cheap products flooding markets? That ship sailed at the beginning of this century. More important than being dominant in trade to a society, is an obligation to make sure the residents in your nation are governed with policies that promote equitable shares in a country's resources, wealth management, and safety and health provisions, in a robust democratic republic. In which citizens know their voices and lives make a difference in how people in power treat us, and that the powerful work to improve everyone's quality of life. Culture wars to divide people are not tolerated; cooperation among nations striving to make our planet more viable to live with is paramount. A dead planet, depleted of clean air, water, and soil, will result in the extinction of humans. The end of abject poverty, hunger, and intolerance over such superficial aspects of humans as physical appearances must be paramount, to help make an end to wars that only enrich weapons makers.

comments.name: Shaun Narine
comments.body: Can we please stop with this nonsense about "excess capacity"? If there were such a thing then every country that exports anything or that develops products for export would have "excess capacity." Quite frankly, the world needs every Chinese solar panel, EV or other green technology that China can produce. The real problem for the rest of the world is that China is simply so big and its industries are so efficient that no one else can credibly compete with it. It has nothing to do with subsidies, something which is very common, including in the US. The problem is not overcapacity, it is overcompetitiveness. That is a different kind of problem. Other countries of the world should decide what industries they want to protect then benefit from the inexpensive, high quality industrial inputs and other affordable consumer goods that China can provide. China's export boom can be an enormous benefit to the entire world, if we allow it to be.

articles.title: The Invisible Way Companies Are Using AI to Set Salaries
articles.summary: New services allow employers to pinpoint who is being paid too much or too little.

comments.name: Paul K
comments.body: Let me guess, this AI analysis doesn't look at the C suite at all--the place with the most overpaid people.

comments.name: R W
comments.body: Use of AI = reversion to the mean.  Because you can use AI doesn't always mean you should.  For example, as the article suggests, a star performer falls in a top bracket so instead it suggests the focus should be on promotion.  This has some potential problems.  As someone who manages hundreds of people and oversees a career service of thousands, some star performers are better left in place and rewarded for their deep domain expertise.  Not all star performers will make good next-level leaders or managers.  Further, what if the focus is on rewarding or reinforcing values and behavior as part of nurturing a quality, high-performing culture; that's a human observable that AI just can't do.

comments.name: R Scott Hughes
comments.body: I am curious how AI could possibly determine which of my employees add the most value.  I have long fought hard for good raises and/or bonuses for the highly valuable and productive members on my team.  It has always been pretty easy to make that argument to the decision makers above me in the organization because I can back it up with data and examples, and I have made sure that my star employees are on the radar of senior management. If I have to argue with AI to justify those raises and bonuses, I am just going to retire.

comments.name: Greg Burke
comments.body: If AI can make these decisions for management... why are we paying for management?

comments.name: Bruce Walker
comments.body: Any business requiring AI to establish pay bands is more clueless than they realize.  Higher paid employees are almost always compensated better in part to prevent other organizations from hiring them away.  Minus that competitive reason for paying them more, productivity and contribution play a far smaller role than many realize.  Yet AI is supposed to benchmark them against this limited criteria along with a data set collected full of bogus information about what other companies are allegedly paying from phantom job postings.

comments.name: WiL O
comments.body: I can bet that won't include top layer mgmt, only the minions salaries.

comments.name: Dennis Conley
comments.body: Mercer and other compensation‑consulting firms have been providing granular workforce and pay‑structure data for decades. In the 1990s, I relied on Mercer’s datasets to conduct the same type of analysis now being described as “AI‑enabled.” The underlying work - benchmarking roles, modeling pay bands, and comparing market competitiveness - is not new. What is new is the branding. Companies are repackaging long‑standing analytical practices under the AI umbrella, often overstating the role of machine learning in processes that historically depended on structured surveys and human interpretation. The story here isn’t an AI revolution; it’s the industry’s tendency to re‑label established methodologies to match the moment.

comments.name: CAK
comments.body:
With all the news that has already been reported from around the country about data center violations, it is astounding to learn about what they continue to get away with as they are being developed.

City, county and state officials need to be on full alert with very frequent (weekly?, monthly?) site inspections to check for permits or lack thereof and other possible violations of zoning, environmental, electrical, water, noise and other restrictions and requirements. Because inspections require funding, the fees should be appropriately set to cover all necessary and reasonable government monitoring and actions.

Nearby neighbors also need to be well informed (self, news and government) about all permitting and other restrictions and requirements and there should be easy ways for them to officially question or report about any potentially suspicious or disturbing activities at data center sites.

Violations, especially willful violations of any type, should be heavily fined and it should be easy to quickly shut down operations (including development and functional operations) whenever that seems appropriate, such as for additional inspections and evaluations as well as for submitting required plans and information or for obtaining required permits, especially ignored permits. Data centers should not be allowed to get away with  for not doing what's rightfully expected of them to protect the environment and the quality of life and community and its energy and water supplies.

comments.name: Steve S
comments.body:
Data centers are 24 hour operations; humans need sleep. The elephant did care where it stepped, the thing underneath  being too small to be very inconvenient. Such elephants need training in kindliness.  

It seems to me that the state has a role in noise abatement that includes payments to residents. The state could monitor noise levels and variations, such as the starts and stops that make the noise hard to ignore, and either have a direct-to-residents payment scheme built into the law or mechanism that would organize a class action suit for everyone in the affected area.

We would go up on the rim to Nordic ski all day, and then come back down to our camp in the Valley and cook dinner. Since it got dark early in winter, we often went to the bar in the Awanahee Hotel, which is the antithesis of free camping. Currently a room, with not much of a view, is $820/night.  We would sit in a corner in the great room by the huge fireplace, play cards or chess, and drink a few hot toddies. Then back to our tents by 10. The staff tolerated us - we looked pretty rough but were polite.The great thing about National Parks in the US is that everyone has a right to be there. Canada's predicament. China and the European Union are both global economic powerhouses, their high-value import dependencies reflect opposite sides of the industrial spectrum: China relies on Western and East Asian suppliers for advanced "upstream" technologies—specifically cutting-edge semiconductors, lithography equipment (ASML), precision CNC machinery, jet engines, and patented biopharmaceuticals and the EU relies on foreign imports for "downstream" hardware and digital services, depending heavily on the US for cloud computing, AI platforms, enterprise software, and defense avionics, while importing advanced microchips, consumer electronics, lithium-ion battery cells, rare-earth magnets, and active pharmaceutical precursors (APIs) from East Asia.
Canada’s economic offering to the global market rests primarily on its role as a resource superpower, boasting vast reserves of raw energy (crude oil, natural gas, uranium), critical minerals (unrefined nickel, lithium, cobalt, and potash), and soft commodities (timber, grains, and freshwater). Beyond primary extraction, Ottawa offers specialized high-end capabilities in niche sectors—most notably world-class academic research in artificial intelligence and quantum computing, specialized aerospace engineering, and advanced financial services. However, its primary leverage on the world stage remains that of a premier, reliable supplier of upstream natural resources and essential industrial feedstocks.

I can't help but notice that we are all using the internet, we are all using phones, tablets, and laptops, to write these comments, which all require these critical minerals. I doubt any of us are going to cut back on our technology dependence to save the environment we care so much about. Yet, we have a CEO coming along, telling us there is a better way to mine the same critical minerals, while protecting more of our precious ecosystems, and people want it stopped. It is true that there are more unknowns related to deep sea mining than traditional land-based mining. We are well aware of what we are destroying on land. 1,000 to 3,500 hectares of forest directly cleared per 1M tonnes of Cobalt. 2,000 to 5,000 hectares of tropical forest strip-mined per 1M tonnes of Nickel. 500 to 1,500 hectares of high-elevation fragile soils and scrubland per 1M tonnes of Copper. 300 to 1,200 hectares of rainforest per 1M tonnes of Manganese. This combines for 3,800 – 11,200 hectares of direct land, completely destroyed, for these 4 minerals. TMC wants to operate a vacuum over just 900 – 1,700 hectares for the same amount of minerals. The ocean floor will not be completely destroyed either, as studies have shown that life and ecology does return. This choice seems simple to me.

I became a fan in midlife, largely through my daughter, and I loved taking her to the Eras Tour. But The Life of a Showgirl was such a disappointment that it feels like a turning point.

Swift seems to have lost touch with the fans who helped build her career, along with any pretense that she isn’t just another billionaire hawking the latest product. TLOASG felt vapid and, dare I say, lazy compared with the wit, specificity, and emotional intelligence of her best songwriting. The showgirl imagery also bothers me: this isn’t transgressive feminist empowerment; it’s the boring, age-old pursuit of the male gaze.

And then there’s the relationship with her fans. Swift built an extraordinary empire in part by cultivating intimacy, sharing her life, leaving clues, inviting fans to feel as though they were along for the ride. Now even wedding photos are apparently off-limits, despite what was hardly presented as an exercise in quiet anonymity.

Of course, she’s entitled to privacy. She’s entitled to make whatever music she wants. And she certainly doesn’t owe fans access to her wedding. But fans are equally entitled to notice when the relationship that made the whole enterprise so powerful begins to feel markedly more transactional.

The spell is broken. My household has moved on.

Artists like Billie Eilish, Sabrina Carpenter (on her first album), and Chappell Roan all make much more interesting and fresh music – while presenting as irresistibly pop.

I have always admired artists who have a restrained approach to releasing music. Like The Killers, who, I believe, talked about writing forty or more songs per album before choosing around twelve of them for release. See also Dolly Parton, who has talked about her drawers overflowing with songs. To me, that demonstrates great craftswomanship. Writing music and releasing music are two separate things. The maximalist approach to albums, when they're overstuffed but not very nourishing, doesn't make sense to me. Not all of your song-shaped journal entries need to reach our ears. comments.name: Steven Walker
comments.body: The argument that this test hadn't been proven to reduce deaths is completely ridiculous. Thinking it through, anyone who understands the severe lmiitations of randomized controlled trials to answer a question that is confounded by everything that happens between detection, treatment and death, would realize that the question can't be answered reliably with that kind of trial. Further, it would take many years to produce a result and the purists would want separate results for each type and even stage of cancer at diagnosis. We know that early detection saves lives in a lot of cancers, and we know that many cancers are not detected until the patient experiences symptoms severe enough to get them to a doctor that actually diagnosis the disease, often too late.  Even if the test doesn't detect every cancer, it will detect a lot of them, and some early enough to save lives. Approve it, and in the meantime let's work harder to purge the statistical purists in medicine and at the FDA who won't believe anything until they have counted enough deaths to declare statistical significance. That meaningless metric they worship, a thing called a p- value, has killed a lot of people over the decades by causing them to have to wait too long for the treatment they needed. This test could get them to that treatment a lot faster.

comments.name: Wendy B.
comments.body:
Many screening tests for cancer have been discarded because they cause more harm than good. False-negatives lead people to think they are cancer-free and thus they ignore symptoms and false-positives lead to invasive tests, mental anguish, and often, harmful over-treatment. 
This blood test is likely to lead to massive amounts of harm and very little good because it is not very accurate. 
The other problem is that many people naively believe that finding cancer early is always a good thing, but it isn't. The majority of blood-test based cancer tests so far have only been able to detect extremely malignant cancers that shed cells into the bloodstream. These cancers are untreatable, regardless of when they are detected. If you detect them early, the patient will undergo massive amounts of futile treatment and then die. If you detect them late, the patient will go on hospice and then die at the exact same time, but they were able to enjoy their last two or three years of life, unlike the early detector.

comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
Because the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle has the attention, and there's more pacific huricanes, the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMOC or AMO) is no less important.

AMOC is the long-term natural cycle of Atlantic water--warm surface water travels north, cools and sinks near the pole, and circulates. It helps keep N. Europe warm winters. And helps drive huricane formation, along with a smaller cycle of downwelling and upwelling off Africa called Little El Niño.

https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/amoc.html

https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/the-atlantic-nino-el-ninos-little-brother/ 

These cycles are not caused by climate change but are also not independent. Warmer air above warmer oceans fuel storms & huricanes, warmer air holds more moisture, it's a positive feedback.

Oceans are absorbing a lot more heat energy, causing temperature gradients to increase at deeper depths. The long-term impact on ocean cycle turnover is not clear; modeling shows continued warming reduces water density (boyancy), increases stratification and suppresses surface water from cooling and sinking.

The AMOC has been weakening, the cause is not clear but models show continued warming collapses the AMOC with dire consequences.

The climate system is complex, with many interacting componants and feedbacks.
Observation and modeling indicate human forced climate change has impacted many natural cycles. Many natural systems are now unstable. It's hightime to prevent the worst consequences.

Seeing how we are already seeing much more rapid intensifications of tropical cyclones at our current temperature of around 1.4 deg C above preindustrial times I became curious to see what tropical cyclones would be like as the Earth gets hotter.

So I asked Gemini about it and here’s the response. (For fun you should ask AI about storms at 6 deg C).

"At a 3°C global temperature rise, tropical cyclones will undergo severe behavioral shifts:

Hyper-Intensification: Total storm frequency may drop, but a drastically higher percentage will reach Category 4 and 5. Explosive 24-hour intensification will become the norm rather than the exception.

Catastrophic Rainfall: Warmer air holds exponentially more moisture, triggering unprecedented rainfall rates and severe flooding.

Inland Devastation: Warmer, wetter continental environments will cause storms to decay much slower after landfall, driving hurricane-force winds deep into inland territories.

Poleward Expansion: Expanding ocean heat will shift storm tracks poleward, threatening coastal regions and cities historically unaccustomed to extreme hurricanes.

Compounding Surges: Severe baseline sea-level rise means even average storms will push catastrophic storm surges much further inland.

At 3°C, tropical cyclones will routinely reach the absolute upper thermodynamic limits of destructive power."

Getachew Reda mentioned in the article, once a prominent Tigray leader who defended Tigray in the 2020-2022 war as an act of survival for the people of Tigray, he has now switched sides to work for Abiy. And that in itself is not a bad thing if it would facilitate the making of peace between Ethiopia/ Abiy and Tigray. 

However, what makes Getachew a tragic political figure is that he has reduced himself to denouncing Tigray leaders (TPLF), without offering a political solution - such as, would Abiy allow displaced Tigray people to return to their homes. And can Getachew persuade Abiy to have a project for Tigray economic reconstruction and revival.

comments.name: Hillside
comments.body:
The 2020-2022 conflict was Ethiopia/Abiy's war of choice intended to eliminate Tigray political leaders (TPLF). Instead, it degenerated into a war of death and displacement, a siege, and the use of starvation as a weapon against the people of Tigray. It was intensified by tribal animosity, Amhara against Tigray.

The peace deal reached in 2022 provided an understanding for Abiy and TPLF to hold discussions for a political settlement. However later, Abiy refused to deal with TPLF, consigned Tigray to an interim administration without end, with no participation in national elections, no representation in the parliament.  

Abiy would not work with TPLF to reintegrate Tigray back into Ethiopia as a full-fledged region in the country, leaving Tigray in a state of suspended political existence, culminating into this new outbreak of conflict. A clear case of the same poor political leadership, for a second time.

Approaching 420 ppm CO2 and a rise of 1.2 C degrees above pre-industrial temperature - very close to what we actually got in 2020.

Also when the characters seem real or like reality tv but not it makes it so interesting.

comments.name: Frank
comments.body: Let me be frank, as a lover of many TV shows and movies there are few that consistently grab my attention-and heart-like the beloved comedy The Office does. Many attribute the popular sitcom to a few successful seasons of dry, sarcastic humor, boring characters, and mundane plot but I am here to say that this assumption couldn't be further from the truth. The plot line is complex and the characters undergo years worth of development throughout the series. The viewers witness relationships (romantic and platonic alike) crumble and thrive all within the confines of a fluorescent-lit office space. The Office is so unique because of how it captures something many Americans are so familiar with, yet makes it an entirely new way of experiencing a 9 to 5. The characters also become more like a family than coworkers and this adds to a sense of comfort that viewers feel when watching. The Office is a well constructed, equal parts hilarious and heartbreaking, TV show. There is nothing that is quite like it-producers try as they might.

When you go on an interview, most interviewers ask if you'd like something to drink.

I was always told if asked, "Would you like water, tea, or coffee?"--as most offices have these--that I should accept the water.

Generally, you get bottled water, and that is great--especially if your mouth goes dry during a long interview.

Also, I was told that the ask / accept dynamic establishes a pleasant bond at the start. 

The interviewer is also your host, and your acceptance of their offer is a kind way to acknowledge their thoughtfulness.

If you bring your own drink, you're making it harder to establish that initial bond via the ask / accept.

It can be smart to inject before travel so you don't have to worry about taking medicine with you if the trip is under a week. Side effects are not an issue if you are on a given dose and continuing, but I would not taper up just before a trip.
